title: Morphology Manipulation of Cu Nanocrystals and Product Selectivity in Electrocatalytic Reduction of Carbon Dioxide
abstract: We have revealed that cube-like and hexarhombic docadehedron-like Cu single-crystals showed an enhancement of C2 products (ethylene and ethanol) while octahedron-like Cu nano single-crystals promoted C1 products of CO2 reduction. This product selectivity was revealed to be highly associated with the atomic arrangement on the surface. The remarkable high selectivity of ethanol (faraday efficiency 25% with 14 mA/cm2, Jethanol ~3.5 mA/cm2) for H-Cu was investigated and unraveled by using in-situ X-ray absorption spectroscopy and density functional theory (DFT) calculation. It was shown that the binding energy of adsorbed *O atom on the surface is substantial, which cause the bifurcation of reaction pathway and leads to the formation of ethanol.

KEYWORDS: electrocatalysis; CO2 reduction; Cu nano single-crystals; ethanol oxametallacycle
Electrocatalytic reduction of carbon dioxide (CO2) has attracted considerable attention in past couple decades due to its great potential in the field of sustainable energy and carbon neutrality. With the integration of renewable energy (e.g., solar energy or wind power), it can serve as an efficient approach to convert CO2 into useful fuels such as methane (CH4), ethylene (C2H4) and ethanol (CH3CH2OH).[1-9] Hori et al., Azuma et al. and others have done many pioneering works to explore the ability of electrocatalytic CO2 reduction for various bulk metals in aqueous media systematically.[10-14] Copper (Cu), according to these studies, is the only electrocatalyst that can reduce CO2 to hydrocarbon products with acceptable current density (~5 mA/cm2).[12, 15, 16] In addition, it was realized that the distribution of these products is potential-dependent, and highly associated with the surface conditions such as roughness, grain boundary and crystal facet of Cu metal.[1727] Especially for the crystal facet, Hori et al. and Takahashi et al. have indicated that Cu(100) facet can facilitate the formation of ethylene while Cu(111) facet would favor methane generation.[26, 27] It was also reported that the Cu(110) facet could enhance the yield of ethanol and acetic acid.[28] These results are fascinating and provide valuable insights to the mechanism of electrocatalytic CO2 reduction. However, in those studies, the surface treatments (e.g., electropolishing and annealing) of bulk
copper material were rather radical,[12, 26-28] which would induce undesired surface reconstruction of the copper electrode and veiled the intrinsic product selectivity for different crystal facets of copper electrodes.[6]

their catalytic activities at atomic level. In this work, we have synthesized three different shapes (Figure 1a) of copper nano single-crystals with desired facets. The cube-like, hexarhombic docadehedron-like and octahedron-like Cu nano single-crystals (hereafter denoted as C-Cu, H-Cu and O-Cu, respectively), were subjected to investigating their ability of electrocatalytic CO2 reduction in aqueous media (KHCO3). It was revealed that the product distribution was highly related to surface orientation (crystal facets) as well as electrolyte concentration. C-Cu could boost ethylene evolution of CO2 reduction while O-Cu could increase the production of carbon monoxide and methane. HCu, to our surprise, could reduce CO2 and produced large amount of ethanol (Faraday Efficiency, F.E. ~25 % at 14 mA/ cm2 Jethanol ~3.5 mA/ cm2). Although such high ethanol conversion efficiency is not unprecedented. This result is still quite intriguing since most electrocatalysts showing high ethanol efficiency are either copper oxide derived particles (Cu2O) or copper alloys.[15, 16, 27, 29-42] Understanding the reason for this product selectivity (ethanol) of H-Cu could be very helpful and sheds a light on the direction of designing new electrocatalyst to control the product of CO2 reduction. In addition, to the best of our knowledge, this is the first work reports electrocatalytic CO2 reduction using well-defined Cu nanocrystal except C-Cu (we also include C-Cu in this work for comparison).[36-41] Therefore, we decided to embark a more detail investigation on the surface atomic arrangements of these Cu nano single-crystal samples and their correlation with respect to product selectivity of electrocatalytic CO2 reduction.
As shown in Figure 1a, these samples have distinct 2- dimentional shapes, which are square, hexagonal and rhombus for C-Cu, H-Cu and O-Cu, respectively. The 3- dimentional morphology of these samples were also examined and confirmed that C-Cu is cube-like and H-Cu has hexarhombic dodecahedron-like configuration (Figure S1). For O-Cu, it shows an octahedron-like appearance. As a result, it can be assumed that the shape of C-Cu is comprised of 6 Cu(100) planes with 12 edges. H-Cu is consisted of 4 Cu(100) and 8 Cu(111) planes with 28 edges, while O-Cu is made of 8 Cu(111) planes and 12 edges. The representative crystal structures for these three samples were illustrated in Figure 1 (bottom). In addition, the powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) patterns of these samples (Figure 1b) display very strong preferred orientations when depositing on Si wafer substrate. The PXRD pattern of C-Cu barely shows (111) diffraction peak but only (100) one. O-Cu, in contrast, exhibits very high ratio of (111) over (100) peak intensity. The situation for H-Cu is similar to that of O-Cu except that the intensity of (111) over (100) is slightly lower. The difference ratio on peak intensity (i.e. (111) to (100)) among these samples are owing to their preferred orientations (particle arrangement) on the substrate, which it also supports the morphology analysis from TEM (Figure 1a) and SEM images (Figure S1). It is worth mentioning that there is a noticeable contrast difference on the fringes of H-Cu (Figure 1a bottom, colored in green), which suggests a step surface. With the aims of examining this feature and the surface atomic arrangement of C-Cu,
H-Cu and O-Cu. These samples were inspected by using high-resolution transmission electron microscope (HRTEM) and the images with corresponding explanations for each sample were displayed in Figure S2 and S3.
After revealing the morphology and atomic arrangement on the surface of these samples, these Cu samples were deposited on L-shape glassy carbon electrodes to conduct their electrocatalytic CO2 reduction abilities in 0.1 M KHCO3 (In Figure 2a-c). The loading amount of C-Cu, H-Cu and O-Cu sample on electrode was checked by using ICP-MS and the amount is roughly the same for each sample (Figure S4). The detail electrochemical measurement setups and product analyzing methods were provided in Supporting Information. The potentials in this context were all converted to relative hydrogen electrode (RHE). The product quantification was mainly utilizing gaschromatography (GC), gas-chromatography cou pled with mass spectrometry (GC-MS) and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) technique.
The calibration curves for concentration of gas and liquid products of CO2 reduction along with their representative signals were also included in supporting information (Figure S5–S7). Moreover, it is known that only the F.E. of CO2 reduction is insufficient to reflect the performance of electrocatalyst. It has to combine with the

Therefore, time– dependent current density curves at selected potentials of electrocatalytic CO2 reduction was also plotted and shown in Figure S8. The potential (V vs RHE)–dependent partial current density curves of CO2 reduction products (F.E., > 5%) of electrocatalytic CO2 reduction for Cu samples was provide in Figure S9 and the morphology of these Cu samples after chronocoulometry test were also examined and shown in Figure S10.
In Figure 2, for all three samples at low cathodic potential (> –0.85 V), the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) dominates in this potential window. The major products for CO2 reduction are formic acid (HCOOH) and carbon monoxide (CO), while we also detected methane (CH4) and ethylene (C2H4) at potential around –0.8 V, although the amount is very low (F.E. < 0.1 %). With decreasing the potential from –0.85 V to –1.0 V, the amount of hydrogen and formic acid starts to decrease while the concentration of carbon monoxide increases and reaches to maximum at a potential around -0.95 V. In the range of -1.0 V to -1.2 V, the F.E. contribution from CO2 reduction reaction begins comparable to that of HER. The F.E. contribution of carbon monoxide (CO) starts to decline while the quantity of hydrocarbon products (i.e. CH4, C2H4 and CH3CH2OH) begins to increase. This phenomenon implies that the carbon monoxide could be one of the critical intermediates and would further act as paramount roles for generating hydrocarbon product at higher cathodic potential region (< –0.95 V).[12]
Figure 3. In-situ X-ray absorption spectra of Cu K-edge for CCu (a), H-Cu (b), O-Cu (c) samples in an neutral aqueous solution containing (0.1 M KHCO3) and in an in-situ liquid cell.
The bottom panel shows the difference spectra of various applied potentials based on the condition of -0.3 V.
In terms of their CO2 reduction selectivity toward hydrocarbon products, remarkable differences can be readily identified for C-Cu, H-C and O-Cu samples. The F.E. of ethylene for C-Cu is significantly higher than that of H-Cu and O-Cu. It remains above 30 % from –1.05 V to –1.2 V and above 20 % from –1.0 V to –1.3 V. This high F.E. of ethylene across such wide potential window of C-Cu is coincident with previous studies and shows a solid evidence that Cu(100) facet prefers to convert CO2 to ethylene.26, 39 The H-Cu, unexpectedly, could reduce CO2 to ethanol with F.E. ~25 % at –1.2 V and with F.E. above 10% from –1.15 V to –1.25 V. These values are remarkably higher than that of C-Cu, O-Cu and bulk Cu in the same potential range.[12, 16] Moreover, we also notice that the F.E. for ethylene and ethanol follows the same trend across the measured potentials, suggesting that the formation of ethylene and ethanol may share the same reaction pathway as well as key intermediates (Figure 2 and S9).[27, 43, 44]
The product distribution of the CO2 reduction for OCu (Figure 2c) is roughly resemble to that of H-Cu except for carbon monoxide and ethanol, where the highest F.E. of carbon monoxide (~25 %) and lowest F.E. of ethanol (< 10%) for O-Cu among these samples across the measured potential range. Notice that the F.E. of methane is lower than that of ethylene until potential around –1.15 V. This result is quite puzzling because it is different to the observations in previous studies that Cu(111) facet is beneficial to reduce CO2 to methane.[13, 35] It suggests other important factors (e.g. electrolyte concentration, particle size or edge effect) that may be still missing and significantly influences the product distribution of CO2 reduction to causes this discrepancy. Notice that Reske et al. clearly demonstrated that the product selectivity of CO2 reduction for using nonfaceted spherical Cu nano-particle is very different from that of using bulk Cu material.[13, 35, 36] To further elucidate this point and the association between the morphologies (i.e., Cu(100) and Cu(111) facets) and the formation of methane/ethylene (i.e., C1 and C2 products). The C-Cu and O-Cu samples were subjected to examining their electrocatalytic CO2 reduction performance in a higher concentration electrolyte (0.5 M KHCO3), in which the C-Cu sample displays a relative high ethylene production comparing to that of methane in the low cathodic potential area (> –1.0 V) while, for O-Cu, the detected content of methane is higher than that of ethylene in nearly all potential range (Figure S11). Apparently, regardless the influence of catalyst morphology, methane is a favored product of CO2 reduction in the high cathodic potential region under concentrated KHCO3. This has shown that the concentration of the electrolyte is another essential role in the CO2 reduction reaction.[12, 41, 45]
Based on the product analysis mentioned above, there are some similarities and differences between these Cu nano-crystal samples. It will be interesting to monitor their electronic states and bonding environment during CO2 reduction reaction. Therefore, we performed in-situ X-ray

The normalized XANES (X-ray absorption near edge structure) spectra of the C-Cu, H-Cu and O-Cu samples were shown in Figure 3, the edge-shape which resulted from the transition from the 1s into the 4p like orbitals was similar for all samples. The well-pronounced feature of the absorption edge under various potentials were visible and significantly different from those of either CuO or Cu2O references, revealing that the as-prepared shaped Cu nanostructures were characteristic of metallic nature rather than copper oxide.
The origin spectrum feature of H-Cu slightly differed from those of C-Cu and O-Cu samples, which could be attributed to the specific bonding environment with a different crystalline geometry. The XANES features as illustrated in Figure 3 were denoted as P (pre-edge) as well as four distinct peak-like structures (denoted A to D), where no remarkable pre-edge feature that caused by a dipole transition from 1s to the mixing states of 4p and 3d could be visible and suggested a centro-symmetry nature of copper.[46] This phenomenon also indicated that the copper atoms were characteristic of metallic crystal with a face-centered cubic system (centro-symmetry) as revealed in Figure 1b. Furthermore, the difference spectra of various applied potentials based on the condition of -0.3 V (Figure 3 bottom) revealed that a significant interaction with 4s orbital under larger cathodic potential (> –0.9 V) for H-Cu, while both C-Cu and O-Cu exhibited the major binding with 4p orbital rather than evident interaction with 4s one. This phenomenon suggested a different behavior for H-Cu comparing to that of C-Cu and O-Cu during the CO2 reduction reaction.
Figure 4. The calculated formation energy of *OCH2CH (set as zero point), *OCH2CH2, CH3CHO, *O and C2H4(g) on Cu(100) and Cu(110). The oxygen atom was showed in red sphere while dark and light grey sphere represented carbon and hydrogen atom, respectively. The Cu atoms were colored in green and orange for Cu(100) and Cu(110), respectively. In order to emphasize the binding environment between these facets and adsorbed species. The color of Cu atoms in first layers was changed to white except those coordinated to adsorbed species (interatomic distance < 2.3 Å).
The morphology of these Cu nano single-crystals indeed showed critical influence on product selectivity of CO2 reduction. The high F.E. of ethanol for H-Cu is especially intriguing. Takahashi et al. concluded that ethanol was a favored CO2 reduction product by using Cu(110) single-crystal as electrode.[16] It’s well-known that the atomic arrangement along the edge side of the nanoparticle can be regarded as (110) facet (Figure S12). Based on the geometry, H-Cu possesses the greatest number of edges (28 edges) among three Cu nano singlecrystal samples and the observed step surfaces in H-Cu would also increase the number of edges. The most edges (i.e. Cu(110) facet) in H-Cu could be a plausible explanation for the elevated yield of ethanol in electrocatalytic CO2 reduction. Although the mechanism of converting CO2 to ethanol has not been fully understood yet, Calle-Vallejo and Koper suggest that the step reducing the adsorbed *CH2CHO to CH3CHO (l) (further reduce to ethanol) or to C2H4 and adsorbed *O could be a vital bifurcating point for ethylene or ethanol formation from electrocatalytic CO2 reduction.[32] Accordingly, to explicate the high selectivity of ethanol formation for H-Cu (more edge sides, e.g. Cu(110) facet), we performed theoretical calculation based on the approach of Calle-Vallejo and Koper’s work. To be concise, we only compute the key step that split the pathway from ethylene to ethanol. In Figure 4, the formation energy of adsorbed *O and C2H4 on Cu(100) surface is lower than that of CH3CHO(l) by ~0.25 eV and suggests ethylene is a preferred product reducing from *CH2CHO. This result is in good agreement with the work of Calle-Vallejo and Koper. The case in Cu(110) surface, in contrast, favors a route to produce CH3CHO(l), which could be readily reduced to ethanol[19] and explains the increased selectivity of ethanol for H-Cu.
We have to note here that original intention of performing in-situ XAS experiment is to probe the structural and electronic information of these Cu nano single-crystals during electrocatalytic CO2 reduction. Moreover, this information could link to possible intermediate from DFT calculation. Although the in-situ XAS spectrum of these Cu nano singlecrystals indeed behave differently, and this result was reconfirmed with ex-situ XAS experiment (Figure S14). Considering the CO2 reduction is a very complex reaction and many intermediates could “co-exist” during reaction. It is still unlikely to offer any concrete conclusion at current stage. More sophisticated investigation (e.g. in-situ Raman and FTIR)[47] and DFT calculation (with solvent and electric field effect)[48] on these Cu nano single crystals are underway and will be discussed in the future. Moreover, based on the comparison between Figure 1 and Figure S10, although the morphology and the shape of these Cu nanocrystal samples are mainly preserved (< 60 mins or reach to ca. 20 Coulombs), but the exposed facets have slightly diminished. This suggests that the dynamic evolution of the catalysts is very important for time resolved product distribution analysis and corresponding product selectivity to as-synthesized morphology, especially for designing practical electrode and operating in industrial time scale. This result also offers an important illustration of understanding the catalysis of Cu nanocrystals but not a practical strategy for synthesizing practical electrodes.

In summary, through controlling the morphologies of Cu nano single-crystals, we have demonstrated that the atomic arrangements on theses Cu sample surface is crucial toward product selectivity of electrocatalytic CO2 reduction. The C-Cu (mainly Cu(100) facets) could facilitate C-C coupling and generate C2 product (ethylene), while O-Cu (mainly Cu(111) facets) would favor different mechanism for CO2 reduction reaction. H-Cu showing higher selectivity toward ethanol is quite unexpectedly since the surfaces comprise Cu(100) and Cu(111) facets. This result could be attributed to the higher edge sides (i.e. Cu(110)) and DFT calculation suggests that the less stability of adsorbed *O on the Cu(110) surface could cause the spilt of the reduction pathway from ethylene to ethanol.
